analysis.one_liner: Bans new large factory farms, phases out existing ones by 2040, and curbs big meatpackers' control of livestock markets.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 24 House members, never received a committee vote or floor vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would freeze new large factory farms (large CAFOs) and shut existing ones down as large CAFOs by 2040, paying owners to exit with transition grants. It would make the big meat companies that control contract farming legally responsible for the pollution and odors those farms create. It would also bar large meatpackers from owning the livestock they slaughter, require at least half of their cattle and hogs to be bought on open spot markets, stop abusive poultry payment 'tournament' contracts, and require meat and dairy to carry country-of-origin labels, with 'Product of U.S.A.' reserved for animals born, raised, and slaughtered here.
analysis.who_benefits: Small and midsize livestock farmers and contract growers, who would gain leverage against the large meat companies they contract with; rural residents living near large factory farms, who would see new ones blocked and existing ones phased out with pollution liability shifted to the integrator companies; and shoppers, who would get clearer country-of-origin labels on beef, pork, and dairy.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small farmers, contract growers, rural residents

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits new large CAFOs from starting or expanding and bars existing ones from continuing to operate as large CAFOs after January 1, 2040, with civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation per day.

Creates a voluntary transition program that pays owners of animal feeding operations to pay off farm debt and convert their land to other agriculture, funded by $10 billion per year, in exchange for a permanent easement barring factory-farm use and excessive manure application.

Makes integrators — the large companies that control contract poultry and livestock growing — legally responsible for dead animal and manure disposal, air and water pollution, harm to contract growers, and health, property-value, and enjoyment-of-property harms to neighbors, and makes those duties non-transferable to growers.

Amends the Packers and Stockyards Act to bar large packers from owning or feeding livestock directly (with limited exceptions and transition periods), require at least 50% of their slaughter to come from open spot-market purchases from independent producers, restrict formula-priced forward contracts, and prohibit poultry 'tournament' pay systems that penalize growers for factors outside their control.

Bars packers, swine contractors, and live poultry dealers from withholding pay data from growers, limiting growers' jury rights or remedies, retaliating against growers who assert their rights, or terminating contracts without a lawful basis.

Restores mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef and pork, extends it to dairy products, and allows 'Product of U.S.A.' labels only on meat exclusively derived from animals born, raised, and slaughtered in the United States.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking companies and poultry/livestock integrators, whose ownership of livestock and control of contract growers would be restricted and whose pollution liability would expand; taxpayers, who would fund $10 billion per year in transition grants without an offset; and the large CAFO owners whose operations would be frozen and eventually wound down, though voluntary buyout grants would cushion them.

drawbacks.text: The transition program transfers $10,000,000,000 each year from the Treasury without any offset or appropriation process, an open-ended mandatory cost that grows over the 15-year phase-out.
Voluntary buyout grants would pay operators of large factory farms to exit, which critics could fairly describe as compensating the owners of facilities whose pollution the bill targets.

Phasing out large CAFOs and forcing packers to buy half of their livestock on open spot markets could disrupt existing supply chains and raise meat prices for consumers, at least during the transition.
The ban on packer ownership contains carve-outs for small packers with only one plant and for farmer-owned cooperatives, so the burden falls unevenly across the sector.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's protections for contract growers and its market-power rules address well-documented problems for independent farmers, and the CAFO phase-out with funded transition is a serious attempt to compensate rather than simply displace operators. The main honest objections are the very large unoffset mandatory spending, the buyout payments to CAFO owners, and likely transition-period meat price effects. On balance the design is more carefully built than a simple ban, but the fiscal commitment alone would have made passage contentious even with floor time.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, then to two subcommittees, and neither full committee ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Ro Khanna introduced the bill on May 5, 2020, joined by six original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and, in addition, to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, splitting its provisions between two committees.

The water-pollution provisions were referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment on May 6, 2020, and the livestock provisions to the Subcommittee on Livestock and Foreign Agriculture on August 13, 2020.
No committee markup, hearing, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpacking companies and integrators keep the existing system: no new limits on owning livestock, no spot-market purchase minimums, no expanded pollution liability, and no phase-out of large factory farms. Contract growers and rural neighbors remain under current rules.

for.name: Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Farm System Reform Act of 2020 and recruited six original cosponsors.

for.name: 23 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican did.

against.name: Collin Peterson
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill, which sat referred to his committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the water-pollution provisions to a subcommittee and never acted on them.

against.name: Large meatpacking and poultry integrator companies
against.what_they_did: Opposed measures restricting packer livestock ownership, mandating spot-market purchases, and shifting CAFO pollution liability onto integrators.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 supporters — the sponsor and 23 cosponsors — were House Democrats, with no Republican support and no recorded vote at any stage.

industries.industry: Large meatpacking companies (beef, pork, and poultry slaughter)
industries.note: The bill bars large packers from owning or feeding the livestock they slaughter, requires at least 50% of slaughter to come from open spot-market purchases from independent producers, and restricts formula-priced contracts. These rules would shift bargaining power and price discovery back toward independent farmers.

Integrators would become legally responsible for waste disposal, pollution, harm to contract growers, and damages to neighbors, and could not transfer those duties to growers. Restrictions on tournament pay systems, pay-data disclosure, and one-sided termination would end practices growers say keep them in debt.

industries.industry: Large CAFO operators (industrial dairy, hog, and poultry facilities)
industries.note: New and expanding large CAFOs would be frozen and existing ones phased out as large CAFOs by 2040, but non-integrator owners could voluntarily receive grants to pay off farm debt and convert their operations, with the land placed under a permanent easement.

industries.industry: Small and midsize independent livestock producers
industries.note: Spot-market purchase minimums, the packer ownership ban, and stronger contract protections would give independent producers more buyers and more bargaining power.

Restoring mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef and pork, extending it to dairy, and reserving 'Product of U.S.A.' for animals born, raised, and slaughtered in the United States would end labeling practices that let imported animals carry a U.S. label.
